relationship: Clothing imagery for injustice and curse
rationale: Arrogant people wrap themselves in injustice and ungodliness here; Psalm108 pictures a curse worn like a garment. Both make harmful moral conditions into clothing, while naming different conditions.

The speaker calls his righteous conduct vain while observing prosperous sinners. Malachi reports service to God called futile, outsiders called blessed, and lawbreakers being built up. These distinct clauses support the comparison without merging their subjects.

The psalm asks why God turns away His hand and right hand; Lamentations says He turned back His right hand before the enemy. Both use a turned-hand image in sanctuary-devastation laments, without normalizing the psalm's bosom clause.
Both headings say For the end and concerning Jeduthun. Asaph and David remain their different named authors; no identification with differently spelled Chronicles names is required.
Eyes anticipating the watches correspond to eyes awake before dawn for meditation on God's sayings. The troubled silence here remains distinct from the target's expressly stated meditation purpose.
Speaking at night with one's heart corresponds to the instruction to speak in one's heart, followed by remorse upon one's bed. The searching reflection and bedside remorse remain distinct responses.

The psalm's speaker addresses the people with my law and the words of my mouth; Moses likewise calls Israel to hear the ordinances and judgments he speaks in their ears. This compares teaching addresses without assigning the psalm's first-person voice directly to God.

relationship: Transmission of divine works to children
rationale: The declaration that the wonders were not hidden from the children and the present announcement of God's mighty acts correspond to the command not to forget what Israel saw and to teach sons and sons' sons.
God's established testimony and law are given for fathers to teach their sons; Deuteronomy expressly commands teaching these words to one's sons and speaking them during daily activities.

Testing God by asking food for their souls corresponds to the mixed crowd and Israel craving food and weeping for meat rather than being satisfied with manna. Desire becomes explicit later in the psalm at verses29-30; it is not substituted for souls here.

Psalm105 combines desiring a desire in the wilderness with testing God. Psalm77 combines testing in the heart with asking food for their souls, with desire named later at verses29-30. The related food-testing episode does not erase those differences.

Opening heaven's doors for the ensuing manna contrasts with the officer's mention of heavenly floodgates and his doubt about promised food abundance. His wording is not replaced by an even-if clause, and the wilderness and besieged-city events remain distinct.
The birds fall amid the camp and around its tents; Numbers likewise places the quails all around the camp and describes the people's gathering and cooling them there.
The people deceive God with their mouth and lie with their tongue here; Isaiah exposes lip honor while the heart remains far away. The psalm's next line similarly diagnoses the heart.

God remembers that the people are flesh and a departing spirit. Psalm102 states His knowledge of human formation, calls for remembering human dust, and compares mortal flourishing with grass ended by a passing wind. The imperative and the different nouns are preserved.
The dog-fly that devours the people corresponds to the multitude of dog-flies entering Pharaoh's and his attendants' houses and ruining the land.

The giving of their labors to the locust corresponds to locusts consuming the land's vegetation and remaining tree fruit. The psalm separately assigns fruit to mildew, which is not relabeled as locusts.

Anger through the people's hills and jealousy through their carvings correspond to Moses' description of Israel provoking God with foreign gods and abominations, followed by His jealousy. The psalm's hills and carvings remain its own wording.

relationship: Captured glory in the Shiloh narrative
rationale: The people's strength and beauty are handed to captivity and an enemy in the psalm's Shiloh context; Samuel narrates the ark's capture and Israel's glory carried away. This is a contextual literary correspondence, not a replacement of the psalm's nouns with ark.

relationship: Deaths of the priests in the ark battle
rationale: The priests falling by the sword correspond to the deaths of Hophni and Phinehas when the ark was taken; their priestly office is supplied in 1Samuel1:3. Samuel does not expressly state that the widows will not be wept for, as the psalm does.
The refusal to choose Ephraim's tribe corresponds to God's explicit statement that He threw away all Ephraim's offspring. The psalm additionally names Joseph's dwelling.
The choice and love of Mount Zion correspond to the declaration that the Lord chose Zion and selected her as His dwelling.
God chooses David and takes him from the flocks of sheep here; Samuel narrates the youngest son being fetched from tending the flock and anointed in the midst of his brothers.

David is brought from behind the ewes giving birth to shepherd God's people; God's oracle says He took David from the sheepfold to become ruler over His people Israel. Following the flock is not inserted as an additional phrase in the target.

Maccabees explicitly introduces the flesh of Thy holy ones as part of a written quotation, joining this verse's flesh wording to the blood around Jerusalem and absent burial of the next verse. Its pouring-out wording is preserved.

relationship: Prisoners and sons of those put to death
rationale: Both passages combine the groan of bound people with concern for the sons of those put to death. One petitions for their preservation; the other describes God's hearing and release.

Both headings direct attention to those who will be changed, with yet additionally present in Psalm59. Their other directions and historical notices differ; this correspondence does not identify the Assyrian occasion of Psalm79.
The psalm asks how long God is angry at His servant's prayer; Lamentations describes crying out and calling while God blocks the prayer. Both lament prayer itself encountering divine opposition.

The bread of tears and tears given to drink by measure correspond to the personal lament that tears became the speaker's bread day and night. The measured drinking image is an additional feature here.

Being made an object of contradiction for neighbors while enemies sneer corresponds to being made a reproach to neighbors and scorn and ridicule to surrounding people. Both address God as the One who has placed the community in this humiliation.

relationship: Renewed communal life and response to God
rationale: The assurance that God will give life and the people will call on His name corresponds to Psalm84's affirmation that He will turn back and give life and His people will rejoice in Him. The promised responses differ but both follow communal renewal.

The psalm names God's testing at the water of contention; Numbers names the Water of Dispute, where Israel reviled the Lord and He was shown holy among them. The close water-dispute descriptions are compared without exchanging the parties' different actions.

relationship: Divine speech met by refusal to listen
rationale: Israel's not listening to God's voice corresponds to His complaint that He spoke and called but the people did not listen or answer.

Both passages combine honey supplied from rock with wheat provision. The psalm calls it finest wheat; Deuteronomy names the fat of the kernels of wheat. These particular foods and differing descriptions are preserved.
